newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead no plus in N.C. tobacco country.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead no plus in N.C. tobacco country.

text.p: In eastern North Carolina's Second Congressional District, where tobacco is known as "the golden leaf," candidates of both parties were running against President Clinton's policies as Election Day approached.

Both incumbent David Funderburk, a Republican House freshman who ran on the Contract with America in 1994, and Democratic challenger Bob Etheridge, a five-term state House member, have made tobacco the cornerstone of their campaigns.
Funderburk, 52, hails from the southern end of the district that is home to the famed golf courses of Pinehurst and wealthy retirees who vote Republican.
Etheridge, 55, comes from the other end, which stretches into strongly Democratic Durham and Research Triangle Park.
Couched in between are four Tobacco Belt counties where the battle for the seat likely will be won or lost.

Outraged by Clinton's decision to limit the advertising and sale of cigarettes by regulating nicotine as a drug, Funderburk ralied against the law from the House floor and clashed with its defenders on TV talk shows. He believes Clinton's stand will help him beat Etheridge.
But Etheridge said he also will oppose his party's leadership, since Clinton's decision is so unpopular with tobacco farmers.
"It's a legal product and the president is taking a wrong approach," Etheridge said. "I will continue to fight that."

Analysts said they could not guess at the outcome of the race, with poll data scarce and voters more concerned with hurricane cleanup than politics, after Hurricane Fran caused millions of dollars in damage in the district in September.

"If not for Fran, I think we'd now be seeing high-volume, high-attack, high profile races," said Robin Dorff, a political science professor at North Carolina State University. "It could be pretty ugly."

On Saturday, Etheridge's campaign began airing the first television advertisements referring to an incident a year ago in which Funderburk's car drove another vehicle off the road, leaving three people injured, and then travelled around the block, returning with his wife, Betty, at the wheel, although witnesses claimed they had seen Funderburk driving.

The Funderburks have maintained Betty was the driver when the accident took place, even though David pleaded no contest to driving left of the centre line in exchange for local prosecutors' agreement to drop a separate charge that he lied to police officers about the accident.
Attack advertisements could prove the key to victory in a district where voters often cross party lines.

While registration data shows the tobacco counties' Democrats outnumber Republicans 2-1, recent history shows many of those Democrats vote Republican and have been dubbed "Jesse-crats" for their support of long-term Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, a tireless advocate for tobacco.
Funderburk's voting record is closely aligned with Helms'.
"My voting record fits the people of this district: term limits, a balanced budget, lower taxes and less government," he said. "That's what they want. That's what I give them."
He also supports the death penalty, opposes abortion and wants to make it harder to sue businesses for money damages.

But Etheridge positions are similar. A conservative Democrat, he represents the traits that define the district: a rural swath of conservative, church-going folk who know their neighbours and back tobacco and business.

Etheridge was a basketball star at Campbell University where Funderburk once taught. He built a sizable network of supporters in his four years as a county commissioner, 10 years as state legislator, and eight years as North Carolina superintendent of public instruction -- a post that could do more to derail his chances than Clinton's stand on tobacco.

Funderburk has tried to link Etheridge to a homosexual agenda for children in a recent television advertisement attacking Etheridge for sponsoring an "Unlearning Homophobia," workshop held while he was superintendent, which was designed to help counsellors deal more effectively with gay students.
